newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ICRC chief urges Western military action in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: ICRC chief urges Western military action in Zaire.

text.p: The president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Cornelio Sommaruga, called on Friday for Western military intervention to help aid agencies gain safe access to one million refugees fleeing in east Zaire.
"There is no other option," he told Reuters after a news conference on the humanitarian crisis, when asked if he thought the West should send troops to aid relief.

Speaking at the news conference, Sommaruga appealed to the U.N. Security Council to take urgent measures and said chapter seven under the U.N. charter which authorises member states to use military force, was not ruled out.

"There is an extreme urgency. The victims cannot wait any longer. I would like to recall the responsabilities of the international community. The ICRC is expecting action. It is extremely hard to stay here and not be able to act," he said.

"There are means that can be used. It's up to the international community to make the choice and see to it that humanitarian agencies are able to act," he said. "Global political solutions are needed in this region."
A complex multi-sided war in eastern Zaire has cut off more than one million Rwandan refugees from the outside world and also driven more and more uprooted Zaireans to hunger.

But weeks of hand-wringing by governments and aid agencies have so far produced no international consensus on what can be done in a region where Western powers have little strategic or economic interest.

Sommaruga said the ICRC was in contact with ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels, who have taken large swathes of eastern Zaire, their chiefs and representatives of local armed groups and voiced optimism his agency may gain limited access to the region.

He said the ICRC and other agencies were ready to go into eastern Zaire if their basic security was assured. "We had to quit the region because of pillage, looting and chaos, not because of the conflict. The main problem is that this is more banditry than a war," he said.
Sommaruga called on the international community to assist the refugees where they were by creating protected zones and humanitarian corridors.
"There is an obligation to assist and protect these refugees outside Rwanda, where they are," he said.

"Everyone can observe there's still tension in Rwanda...It's not up to me to say if the situation is right or not to return, but naturally there should be information for refugees on the situation in Rwanda so they can make their own decision."

The Rwandan Hutu refugees, half of them under 16, include tens of thousands of former Rwandan army troops and militiamen who fled their homeland in 1994 after the genocide of up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Armed Hutus, fearing death if they return to Rwanda, now guard what is left of the refugee camps in Zaire and have denied access to outsiders since an insurrection involving Tutsis and other Zaireans cut them off from foreign aid.
